title: Dominic and the Undertow
premise: Gideon Ishikawa has spent seven years writing postcards to the burned-down boarding house where she grew up, addressed to her late grandmother, in a private pidgin of Japanese and English that only the two of them ever spoke. When Mrs. Okabe, the last fluent speaker of the neighborhood's dying creole, asks Gideon to become her final student, Gideon's careful invisibility begins to unravel: the lessons force her to speak, and speaking forces her to remember why the house burned and what she never said to her grandmother. As the demolition date on the vacant lot approaches, Gideon must transcribe Mrs. Okabe's stories into a record no one asked for, confront the estranged uncle who inherited the land, and finally stand on the rubble and say goodbye out loud. She ends not by saving the language alone, but by becoming the one who carries it—reading the last postcard aloud at the demolition, then mailing a new one, this time with a return address.
about_author: Silas Marchetti is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the records of demolished buildings in coastal Pacific towns. This is a second novel, written in the margins of a day job translating property deeds.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. We meet her nightly ritual: composing postcards to the burned boarding house, never mailing them, hiding them in a cigar box. Establish her job transcribing voicemails for a law firm, her silence in meetings, her almost-relationships. Beat: loneliness disguised as discipline; the reader senses the postcards are letters to the dead.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Counts in Two Tongues
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At the corner market she hears Mrs. Okabe arguing with a cashier in the old creole—a language Gideon half-remembers from childhood. Mrs. Okabe recognizes her cadence: 'You're Hana Ishikawa's girl.' She asks Gideon to visit. Beat: recognition as threat; Gideon's invisibility is seen through for the first time in years.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with a letter from Mrs. Okabe interleaved. The first lesson in the cluttered apartment: numbers, names for weather, the word for 'come back.' Mrs. Okabe refuses to let Gideon write anything down. Beat: Gideon's throat locks around the sounds; grief surfaces as irritation, and she storms out—but takes the homework.

chapters.title: What the House Kept
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV in flashback braided with present. The fire seven years ago: the boarding house's destruction, the grandmother's death, the uncle Raymond who signed the insurance papers and vanished. Gideon remembers the last conversation she fled from. Beat: the buried wound opens; we learn her silence began that night, not before.

chapters.title: Raymond Returns
chapters.summary: Gideon and Raymond's POV alternating. The uncle appears at the vacant lot with a demolition permit and a developer's offer—he wants the postcard-writing 'squatter' gone from his property. Gideon, caught on the rubble, lies smoothly for the first time. Beat: power enters the story; inheritance revealed as erasure, and Gideon feels the corrupting pull of her own small deceptions.

chapters.title: The Dictionary of Small Hours
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Mrs. Okabe's health fails; lessons move to the hospital. She reveals she once refused to teach anyone after her own daughter left for the mainland and never wrote back—her invisibility mirrored Gideon's. She asks Gideon to record her, finally. Beat: two keepers of silence negotiate surrender; tenderness with an undertow of urgency.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Raymond's POV. The developer sweetens the deal if the 'heritage angle' can be managed; a university offers Raymond money for Mrs. Okabe's recorded stories—his to sell if he becomes her legal next of kin. Raymond, broke and bitter, begins paperwork to claim her. Beat: corruption made concrete; the language becomes an asset, and Raymond almost believes he deserves it.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Mrs. Okabe is hospitalized permanently; Raymond presents guardianship papers and a consent form signing her recordings over to the developer. Gideon discovers the demolition is moved up—ten days. She confronts Raymond in the hospital corridor and, in the creole, accuses him of theft in front of witnesses. Beat: climax of the power struggle; speaking publicly costs her her invisibility for good.

chapters.title: The Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Mrs. Okabe, lucid one final evening, dictates the ending of the creole's oldest story and tells Gideon the language was never hers to keep—only to pass. She dies at dawn. Gideon writes the postcard she's owed her grandmother for seven years, in full, out loud, standing on the vacant lot the night before demolition. Beat: catharsis; the almost-said finally said.

chapters.title: Return Address
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, six months later. The lot is a foundation pit for condos; Raymond took the money but the university recording, contested and half Gideon's, sits in an archive with her name as contributor. Gideon teaches two children from the old neighborhood in a borrowed church basement, and mails her first postcard in years—addressed to Mrs. Okabe's grave, with a return address of her own. Beat: belonging chosen, not inherited; quiet, earned resolution.
